alt: Five arrow-shaped stages in order: formation (is there a contract?), terms (what was promised?), vitiating factors (is the agreement flawed?), discharge (how did it end?) and remedies (what can the innocent party get?). Problem answers work through only the stages the facts raise, in order.
caption: Formation, terms, vitiating factors, discharge, remedies: the order of every answer.

alt: Three sources of contract rules. Common law: offer and acceptance (Carlill, Adams v Lindsell), consideration (Currie v Misa, Williams v Roffey), intention (Balfour), implied terms (The Moorcock), economic duress (Atlas Express) and damages (Hadley v Baxendale). Statute: the 1999, 2015, 1977, 1967 and 1943 Acts. Equity: specific performance and rescission. Rules are case-based, and statute overrides common law.
caption: Cite a case for common law rules; check whether a statute overrides them.

alt: In Smith v Hughes the seller sold new oats without mentioning age; the buyer privately believed they were old. The court asked what a reasonable person would understand the seller to be promising, so the buyer’s private mistake did not prevent a binding contract. The same objective approach applies to offers, acceptance and intention.
caption: Courts ask what a reasonable person would understand, not what one party privately meant.

alt: Three types of contract and their law: a trader and a consumer make a consumer contract under the Consumer Rights Act 2015; two businesses are governed by UCTA 1977 and common law; two private individuals by common law with limited statutory protection. Section 2 CRA 2015 defines trader and consumer.
caption: Who the parties are decides which statute applies.

alt: Four statuses. Valid: binding and enforceable. Voidable: valid until the innocent party rescinds, as with misrepresentation or economic duress; the right can be lost by affirmation, delay or third-party rights. Unenforceable: valid but not enforceable in court, such as an unwritten guarantee under the Statute of Frauds. Void: no contract at all, such as where there is no acceptance.
caption: The status decides the remedy: rescission for voidable, damages for breach of a valid contract.

alt: Two panels. Bilateral: each party exchanges a promise for a promise. Unilateral: one party promises in return for an act, as in Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co, where £100 was promised to anyone who used the smoke ball as directed and still caught influenza. The type affects when acceptance happens and whether an offer can be withdrawn.
caption: Bilateral: promise for promise. Unilateral: promise for an act.

alt: Asha’s case in five steps: a contract is formed when TechWorld confirms her order; it is a consumer contract under the Consumer Rights Act 2015; the faulty keyboard breaches s9 satisfactory quality; the “No refunds” term cannot restrict her rights under s31; she can use the short-term right to reject within 30 days or seek repair or replacement.
caption: Classify the contract before choosing the statute, then move through the stages.
